title: 5-a-Side vs 11-a-Side Football: Complete Format Comparison 2026
short: Comparing 5-a-side and 11-a-side football formats. Learn rules, field sizes, strategies, and which format suits your team best.
content:
Choosing between 5-a-side and 11-a-side football? This comprehensive comparison covers rules, strategies, benefits, and how to organize matches in both formats using Turfy.

Quick Comparison Overview:

5-a-Side Football:
• 5 players per team (including goalkeeper)
• Smaller field (30m x 20m typical)
• Shorter matches (2x20 or 2x25 minutes)
• Walls/boards instead of touchlines (often)
• No offside rule
• Unlimited substitutions (rolling subs)
• Faster pace, more touches per player

11-a-Side Football:
• 11 players per team (including goalkeeper)
• Full-size field (100-110m x 64-75m)
• Standard matches (2x45 minutes)
• Traditional touchlines and goals
• Offside rule applies
• Limited substitutions (3-5 depending on rules)
• More tactical, position-specific

Detailed Format Breakdown:

1. Field Dimensions

5-a-Side:
• Length: 25-42m
• Width: 16-25m
• Goal size: 3m x 2m (smaller)
• Surface: Often indoor, artificial turf
• Markings: Center circle, penalty area, no halfway line

11-a-Side:
• Length: 90-120m (100-110m standard)
• Width: 45-90m (64-75m standard)
• Goal size: 7.32m x 2.44m (standard)
• Surface: Natural grass, artificial turf
• Markings: Full FIFA markings

2. Player Roles & Positions

5-a-Side Roles:
• Goalkeeper (specific skills needed)
• Defenders (1-2, versatile)
• Midfielders (1-2, box-to-box)
• Forwards (1-2, clinical finishers)
• Everyone attacks and defends
• Fitness crucial (constant movement)

11-a-Side Positions:
• Goalkeeper (specialized)
• Defenders (4, specific roles: CB, LB, RB)
• Midfielders (3-4, DM, CM, AM roles)
• Forwards (1-3, strikers, wingers)
• More position specialization
• Tactical formations important

3. Rules Differences

Offside:
• 5-a-Side: NO offside rule
• 11-a-Side: YES, strict offside enforcement

Substitutions:
• 5-a-Side: Unlimited rolling subs (like hockey)
• 11-a-Side: 3-5 subs max (depending on competition)

Throw-ins:
• 5-a-Side: Often kick-ins or wall play
• 11-a-Side: Traditional two-handed throw-ins

Goalkeeper Rules:
• 5-a-Side: 4-second rule for possession
• 11-a-Side: 6-second rule for possession

Slide Tackles:
• 5-a-Side: Often forbidden (safety)
• 11-a-Side: Allowed if safe

Match Duration:
• 5-a-Side: 2x20 or 2x25 minutes
• 11-a-Side: 2x45 minutes

4. Fitness & Physical Demands

5-a-Side Requirements:
• High-intensity throughout
• Constant sprinting
• Quick direction changes
• Anaerobic fitness crucial
• Less endurance needed
• Recovery time via rolling subs

Average player runs: 4-5km per match

11-a-Side Requirements:
• Endurance priority
• Position-dependent intensity
• Aerobic fitness essential
• Strategic energy management
• Full match stamina needed
• Limited substitution opportunities

Average player runs: 10-12km per match

5. Skill Emphasis

5-a-Side Skills:
✓ Close ball control (tight spaces)
✓ Quick decision making
✓ First-touch quality
✓ Passing accuracy over power
✓ Positioning awareness
✓ Versatility (all players do everything)
✓ Quick reactions

11-a-Side Skills:
✓ Position-specific techniques
✓ Long passing ability
✓ Crossing and heading
✓ Tactical understanding
✓ Stamina and pacing
✓ Set piece execution
✓ Team coordination

6. Cost Comparison

5-a-Side Costs (Per Match/Session):
• Venue rental: $50-100/hour
• Fewer players needed (easier to organize)
• Smaller goals ($100-200 each)
• Less field preparation
• Indoor facility costs

Annual Team Cost: $2,000-4,000

11-a-Side Costs:
• Field rental: $100-300/match
• Full squad needed (11+ players)
• Standard goals ($500-1000 each)
• Field maintenance costs
• More equipment overall

Annual Team Cost: $5,000-15,000

7. Organization & Logistics

5-a-Side Advantages:
✓ Easier to gather 5 players
✓ More frequent matches possible
✓ Indoor facilities weather-proof
✓ Shorter time commitment
✓ Flexible scheduling
✓ Less equipment needed
✓ Simpler tournament organization

11-a-Side Challenges:
- Need 11+ players consistently
- Weather dependent (often outdoor)
- Longer matches (2+ hours total)
- More complex scheduling
- Significant equipment investment
- Tournament logistics complex

8. Strategic & Tactical Differences

5-a-Side Tactics:
• Constant pressure possible
• Man-marking common
• Quick counter-attacks
• Individual skill showcase
• Goalkeeper as extra outfield player
• Formations less rigid
• Common setup: 1-2-1 or 1-1-2

11-a-Side Tactics:
• Zonal defending common
• Formation discipline important
• Build-up play strategic
• Team cohesion critical
• Set pieces major weapon
• Formations define team style
• Common: 4-4-2, 4-3-3, 3-5-2

9. Tournament Formats

5-a-Side Tournaments:
• Can fit 8-16 teams in one day
• Multiple matches per team
• Single venue sufficient
• Popular format: Group stage + knockouts
• Matches: 15-20 minutes
• 3-4 matches per team typical

Example Schedule:
8 teams, 4 hours total
• Groups: 2x10 min each (1 hour)
• Knockouts: 2x12 min (2 hours)
• Finals: 2x15 min (1 hour)

11-a-Side Tournaments:
• Full-day or multi-day events
• 2-3 matches per team typical
• Multiple fields often needed
• Knockout or group formats
• Matches: 2x30-45 minutes
• Longer breaks between matches

Example Schedule:
8 teams, full weekend
• Saturday: Group matches (4-5 hours)
• Sunday: Knockouts + Finals (4-6 hours)

10. Health & Injury Considerations

5-a-Side Common Injuries:
• Ankle sprains (quick turns)
• Pulled hamstrings (sprinting)
• Collision injuries (close quarters)
• Foot/toe injuries (walls, small goals)
• Lower injury severity overall
• Quicker recovery typically

11-a-Side Common Injuries:
• Muscle strains (endurance)
• ACL injuries (cutting, landing)
• Contact injuries (tackles, aerial duels)
• Overuse injuries (longer matches)
• More severe injuries possible
• Longer recovery periods

Which Format is Right for You?

Choose 5-a-Side If:
✓ You have 5-8 available players
✓ Limited time for matches (1-2 hours)
✓ Want frequent play opportunities
✓ Prefer fast-paced action
✓ Budget conscious
✓ Indoor facilities available
✓ Fitness over tactics preferred
✓ All players want maximum involvement

Choose 11-a-Side If:
✓ You have 15+ squad members
✓ Time for full matches available
✓ Want traditional football experience
✓ Emphasize tactical development
✓ Have access to full-size fields
✓ Competitive league participation
✓ Position specialization desired
✓ Prefer strategic team play

Hybrid Option: 7-a-Side

Middle ground between formats:
• 7 players per team
• Medium field (50-60m x 30-40m)
• 2x30 minutes
• Some offsides (usually)
• Mix of tactics and pace
• Popular for youth development

How Turfy Supports Both Formats:

✓ Custom match duration setup
✓ Flexible team sizes
✓ Format-specific statistics
✓ Tournament management for any size
✓ Unlimited rolling subs tracking (5-a-side)
✓ Limited subs tracking (11-a-side)
✓ Match summary cards for both formats
✓ Broadcasting support regardless of format

Tracking Differences in Turfy:

5-a-Side Matches:
• Enable rolling substitutions
• Set 20-25 minute halves
• Focus on individual player impact
• Higher score expectations

11-a-Side Matches:
• Set 3-5 substitution limit
• Standard 45-minute halves
• Position-based analysis
• Standard scoring patterns

Popularity & Trends:

Global Growth:
• 5-a-side growing rapidly (urban areas)
• Futsal (indoor 5-a-side) Olympic consideration
• 11-a-side remains traditional standard
• 7-a-side emerging as youth development format

Urban vs Rural:
• Cities: 5-a-side dominant (space constraints)
• Suburbs/Rural: 11-a-side more common (field availability)

Age Demographics:
• Youth (U12): 5-a-side and 7-a-side preferred
• Teenagers: Mixed, transitioning to 11-a-side
• Adults: Both formats popular
• Veterans (35+): 5-a-side preferred (less running)

Skill Development:

For Youth Players:

Start with 5-a-Side Because:
• More touches per player
• Develops ball control
• Builds confidence
• Less overwhelming
• Everyone involved

Progress to 11-a-Side For:
• Tactical understanding
• Position specialization
• Team coordination
• Competitive development

Transitioning Between Formats:

From 5-a-Side to 11-a-Side:
Challenges:
• Adapting to larger spaces
• Learning positional discipline
• Building endurance
• Understanding offside

Advantages:
• Superior ball control
• Quick decision making
• Comfortable in tight spaces

From 11-a-Side to 5-a-Side:
Challenges:
• Adjusting to faster pace
• Less thinking time
• Defending without offside
• Constant high intensity

Advantages:
• Strong tactical awareness
• Better endurance base
• Set piece knowledge

Conclusion:

Both 5-a-side and 11-a-side football offer unique benefits. Your choice depends on:
• Available players
• Time commitment
• Budget constraints
• Facilities access
• Development goals
• Playing style preference

Many successful teams play both formats:
• 5-a-side for skills and fitness
• 11-a-side for competitive matches

title: Understanding Football Statistics: A Beginner's Guide

content:
Football statistics can seem overwhelming at first, but understanding them helps you analyze performance and improve your game. Here's a beginner-friendly guide to the most important stats.

Basic Match Statistics:

Goals: The most important stat! The number of times a player or team scores.

Assists: When a player makes the final pass that leads directly to a goal. Shows playmaking ability.

Shots: Total attempts at goal. Includes shots on target, off target, and blocked.

Shots on Target: Shots that would have gone in if not saved by the goalkeeper. Indicates accuracy.

Possession: Percentage of time a team controls the ball. Higher possession often means more control of the game.

Passes: Number of successful passes completed. Shows team coordination.

Pass Accuracy: Percentage of passes that reach a teammate. Elite players often have 85%+ accuracy.

Tackles: Defensive actions to win the ball from opponents. Shows defensive contribution.

Interceptions: When a player reads the game and cuts out an opponent's pass.

Advanced Statistics:

Expected Goals (xG): Measures the quality of scoring chances. An xG of 2.5 means a team should have scored 2-5 goals based on their chances.

Key Passes: Passes that lead to a shot. Shows creative ability.

Dribbles Completed: Successful attempts to beat an opponent with the ball.

Aerial Duels Won: Success rate in heading contests.

Clean Sheets: Matches where a goalkeeper/defense doesn't concede a goal.

title: How to Organize a Local Football Tournament (Step-by-Step Guide)

content:
Running a football tournament sounds simple until you're the one doing it. Between team sign-ups, fixture scheduling, tracking scores across multiple matches, and settling arguments about who actually won on goal difference, most first-time organizers end up buried in group chats and half-updated spreadsheets by the second matchday.

Here's how to run one without losing your mind.

1. Pick the Right Format Before Anything Else

Your format decision affects everything downstream: how many matches you need, how long the day takes, and how fair the competition feels.

Round robin works best for 4-6 teams. Everyone plays everyone, so there's no early elimination and the fairest team usually wins. Downside: it takes longer, since every team plays every other team at least once.

Knockout (single elimination) is fastest and creates the most drama, but a team can get eliminated after one bad half. Good for 8+ teams when you need results in a single day.

Group stage plus knockout is the standard for anything resembling a real tournament. Split teams into groups for round robin play, then send the top teams from each group into a knockout bracket. Best balance of fairness and time, but needs more planning.

If you're running this manually, get your format locked in before you open a single group chat. Changing format mid-planning is where most tournaments fall apart.

2. Set Your Team Count and Match Length Based on Time Available

Work backwards from how much time you actually have. A 5-a-side match with two 10-minute halves takes roughly 25 minutes including a break. If you have a 4-hour window, that's realistically 6-8 matches depending on breaks between games and pitch turnover.

Don't overcommit on team count to make the bracket look impressive. A tournament that runs 2 hours over schedule loses players faster than a smaller, well-timed one gains them.

3. Build Your Fixture List Before Matchday, Not During It

This is where most local tournaments go wrong. Someone tries to figure out who plays who on the morning of the event, standing on the pitch with a notepad while sixteen players wait. Build the full fixture list in advance: who plays who, in what order, on which pitch if you have more than one.

For group stage tournaments, this also means deciding your tiebreaker rules ahead of time. Goal difference first, then goals scored, then head-to-head result, is the standard order most local leagues use. Decide this before a dispute happens, not during one.

4. Track Scores, Cards, and Substitutions as They Happen

Whoever is running the scoreboard needs to record goals, cards, and subs in real time, not reconstruct them from memory after the match. This matters for two reasons: disputes get settled instantly if you have a live record, and your standings table updates itself if goal difference and points are calculated automatically rather than by hand at the end of a long day.

This is the single biggest time sink in manually run tournaments. A notebook works until someone disagrees about a card or a sub, and then you're relitigating a match from memory.

5. Keep Standings Visible and Updated Between Matches

Nothing kills tournament energy faster than teams not knowing where they stand. If your format includes a group stage, update the table after every match and make it visible — whether that's a printed sheet on a wall or a live app view players can check on their phones between games.

6. Have a Plan for Disputes Before They Happen

Someone will argue a card should have been a warning, or that a goal didn't cross the line. Decide your dispute process in advance: who has final say, and what evidence settles it (usually whoever recorded the match event live). Announce this at the start, not mid-argument.

title: Round Robin vs Knockout vs Group Stage: Which Football Tournament Format Should You Use?
short: Comparing round robin, knockout, and group stage tournament formats for local football. See which fits your team count, time limit, and fairness goals.
content:
Picking a tournament format is the first decision that shapes everything else about your event: how many matches you need, how long the day runs, and whether the result actually reflects who played best. Here's how the three main formats compare.

Round Robin

Every team plays every other team once. With 5 teams, that's 10 matches. With 8 teams, that's 28.

Best for: 4-6 teams, or situations where fairness matters more than speed. Since every team faces every opponent, results aren't decided by a single bad match or unlucky bracket draw.

Downside: Match count grows fast. Round robin with 8+ teams needs either a full day or multiple simultaneous pitches to finish in reasonable time.

Use it when: You have a small, committed group and want the most accurate ranking of who's actually best, not just who avoided a tough draw.

Knockout (Single Elimination)

Lose once, you're out. With 8 teams, that's just 7 matches total to crown a winner.

Best for: Larger groups (8-16+ teams) where you need a result in a single day, and drama matters as much as fairness.

Downside: A strong team can be eliminated in round one by an off day or a tough early matchup. The format rewards who peaks on the day, not necessarily who's best overall.

Use it when: Time is tight, team count is high, or you want a bracket with genuine knockout stakes from match one.

Group Stage + Knockout

Teams are split into small groups (usually 3-4 teams) for round robin play within the group. Top 1-2 teams from each group advance to a knockout bracket.

Best for: Medium to large tournaments (8-16 teams) where you want fairness in the early stages but still need a decisive knockout finish. This is the format most real tournaments, including the World Cup, actually use.

Downside: More complex to plan. You need to work out group sizes, tiebreaker rules for the group stage, and a bracket seeding method for who plays who in the knockout rounds.

Use it when: You have enough teams and time to justify the extra planning, and want the fairest version of a tournament that still ends in a knockout final.

Quick Decision Guide

Under 6 teams, fairness matters most: round robin
8+ teams, limited time, want drama: straight knockout
8-16 teams, want fairness and a knockout finish: group stage + knockout
Casual pickup with no real stakes: round robin, keep it loose

The moment you're running anything beyond a 4-team round robin, tracking standings by hand becomes the actual bottleneck, not the football. Goal difference calculations, tiebreakers, and knockout seeding all need to update automatically or you'll spend more time doing math on a notepad than watching matches.

title: 5-a-Side vs 7-a-Side vs 11-a-Side: Which Format Fits Your Local League?
short: Choosing a match format for your local football group? Compare 5-a-side, 7-a-side, and 11-a-side on pitch size, player count, and time commitment.
content:
If you're starting a regular football group or setting up a local league, the first real decision isn't the tournament format — it's how many players are on the pitch at once. That choice determines pitch size, minimum player count, match length, and how much of a commitment each session actually is.

5-a-Side

Players needed: 10 total (5 per side), plus subs if you want rotation.
Pitch size: Small, often an indoor court or a small outdoor 5-a-side pitch. Widely available for hourly booking in most cities.
Match length: Usually 2 x 15-20 minute halves.

Best for: Casual weekly groups. Easiest format to fill with a small, consistent group of friends or coworkers. Lowest barrier to organizing since you need the fewest players and smallest pitch.

7-a-Side

Players needed: 14 total, plus subs.
Pitch size: Medium, roughly half of a full-size pitch.
Match length: Usually 2 x 20-25 minute halves.

Best for: Groups that have outgrown 5-a-side but don't have the numbers or pitch access for full 11-a-side. Common format for local leagues and school/university intramural football.

11-a-Side

Players needed: 22 total, plus subs — so realistically 26-30 people committed to show up regularly.
Pitch size: Full-size pitch.
Match length: 2 x 45-minute halves, standard football rules.

Best for: Established clubs and academies with enough consistent players to field two full squads. Highest commitment in terms of player count, pitch booking, and match duration.

Picking a Format for a New Group

If you're starting from scratch, start smaller than you think you need. A 5-a-side group that consistently fills every week is more sustainable than an 11-a-side setup that struggles to find 22 players every Sunday. You can always scale up the format once your group has grown and shown up reliably for a few months.

Whatever Format You Choose, Tracking Still Matters

Smaller formats like 5-a-side often get treated too casually to bother tracking, but that's exactly where stats and simple scoring matter most for keeping a group engaged over time. Who's top scorer this month, who has the best form, and a running head-to-head record all give a casual weekly kickabout a reason to keep showing up.
